chapter_title: The Ailing Planet: the Green Movement's Role

concepts.title: Earth as a Patient: The Holistic and Ecological View
concepts.definition: Nani Palkhivala records the world's shift to a holistic and ecological view: the earth is no longer inert real estate but a living organism -- an ailing patient whose health we hold in trust. The green movement since 1972 turned this view into a worldwide consciousness that redefines our relationship with the planet.
concepts.key_idea: The planet has become a patient -- and humans, first in the dock, must become its physicians.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb104.txt opening sections (green movements role, holistic and ecological view, earth as patient, world as organism rather than machine)
question_patterns: why is the earth called an ailing planet
in class 11 the ailing planet: what is the holistic and ecological view of the world

solution_steps.explain: Earlier ages treated earth as inert matter to be owned and exploited -- a machine to be driven.
The green movement reframed the planet as a living organism whose parts -- air, water, forests, species -- are one body.
Once earth is a patient, humans become caretakers responsible for its survival, not its spoils.

concepts.title: Population, Fisheries and Forests: The Warning Figures
concepts.definition: The chapter gathers hard alarms: human population crossing five billion and racing past sustainable limits, the world's fisheries collapsing under factory ships, and forests -- the planet's lungs and richest habitats -- disappearing faster than they regenerate. Chapter and constitution alike are cited to show we hold the earth in trust for the unborn.
concepts.key_idea: Count the losses -- mouths, nets and saws -- and the arithmetic of depletion becomes undeniable.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb104.txt middle sections (population five billion, fisheries decimated, forests disappearing, tropical forests, constitution earth in trust)
question_patterns: what warnings does the chapter give about population growth
in class 11 the ailing planet: how are the world's fisheries being destroyed
why are forests called important for the planet's health
explain the idea that we hold the earth in trust for future generations

how does development justify itself against the claims of nature

solution_steps.explain: Population growth outpaces the earth's ability to support, making every other claim on nature heavier.
Industrial fishing strips the seas faster than fish breed; chainsaws clear forests faster than they regrow.
Constitutional language treats the earth as held in trust for posterity -- a legal duty to the unborn.

concepts.title: Sustainable Development and the New Economics
concepts.definition: Against the growth-at-any-cost creed the chapter sets sustainable development -- meeting present needs without destroying the basis of future ones. This demands an economics that prices nature, values forests standing as much as felled, and shifts frommore-of-everything to better-within-limits, with man as partner not proprietor of the planet.
concepts.key_idea: Progress must fit inside nature's ledger -- use without spending the capital of the unborn.
concepts.textbook_ref: kehb104.txt closing sections (sustainable development, growth without destroying, new world view, man as partner not proprietor, brandt commission and lester brown mention)
question_patterns: define sustainable development as used in the chapter
in class 11 the ailing planet: why must man become a partner of living things

how can development coexist with the health of the planet
explain the phrase earth in trust with reference to sustainability
what changes in economics does the author advocate

solution_steps.explain: Sustainable development means advancement that leaves future generations the means to advance too.
The ideology of endless material expansion treats finite nature as infinite -- the error behind the ailment.
Man must live as one member of the community of life, valuing whole systems over single harvests.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the significance of the title 'The Ailing Planet' with reference to the green movement's role.

solution_template.explain: The planet figures as a patient showing symptoms -- depleted seas, shrinking forests, warming air.
The green movement is the world's growing self-awareness of this sickness and of human responsibility for it.
Diagnosis has been made; the title urges treatment -- a new, ecological relationship with the earth.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A firm plans to clear a forest for quick profits but also claims to support sustainability. Use the chapter's ideas to evaluate the claim.

solution_template.explain: Sustainable development requires present activity to preserve future capacity; wholesale clearing fails that test.
Man as partner, not proprietor, cannot treat a forest as disposable stock without violating the new world view.
The claim contradicts itself -- profit that liquidates natural capital is the very ailment the chapter warns against.
